work_order.root_cause: There is no write path to gate. The repository has no module between an ActionIntent and a provider write, so every safety property the issue names has nowhere to live: no Intent-Kernel-capability-Executor chain (TR-3), no capability for a kill switch to check (TR-4), no durable nonce for idempotency to dedupe on (TR-5), no trust ledger for posture to be derived from (TR-19), and no fail-closed admission point (TR-24). The approvals screen on top of it is not a degraded version of that machinery; it is a static shape that reads an event type nothing writes and offers buttons nothing listens to.

work_order.approach:
Build the write path as six new tables behind one additive migration, four new pure-or-injected modules, one new domain module, and one composition point, then make every existing consumer of approval, posture or maturity state read through a single definition of each.

1. src/data/db.js adds migration 006 and two PRAGMAs. WAL and busy_timeout go in openDatabase, not in a route: busy_timeout is per-connection, and both the server and the seed process open through this one function, so that is the only place the setting reaches both.
2. src/data/repositories.js adds six repositories behind the same tenant-bound module contract (repositories.js:1-7): approvals (mutable working state, like experiments), capabilities (append-only), actionRecords (append-only on UPDATE, DELETE deliberately allowed - the only reason is named in db.js), killSwitches (mutable), guardianIncidents (append-only), trustLedger (mutable upsert).
3. src/domain/approvals.js is pure: validateApproval, visibleReason, isPendingApproval, partitionApprovals. One predicate decides pending versus lapsed, and four callers (the decide route, the page, the seed reset and the tests) read it instead of four implementations of it.
4. src/policy/kernel.js is the deterministic gate and the only place a write is admitted. Its roster is derived from DECISION_CLASSES by membership and its own render order is pinned, the maturity band is a FLOOR in the direction policyBand's edges already encode, the intent's action is bound to the class that registers it, capabilities are HMAC-signed, and the kill-switch check names the four scope keys it evaluates.
5. src/policy/trust.js derives one posture per class from one stored ledger row and is called by BOTH the rendered table and the gate, so the displayed posture and the enforced posture cannot disagree.
6. src/executor/executor.js is the only module that calls a provider write method, and it dedupes durably in the repository rather than in the per-request fake, which is rebuilt on every request (routes.js:103) and could not survive a second delivery.
7. src/strategy/guardian.js holds the two detectors, the named recovery predicate and the freeze, and freeze takes an explicit scope and scopeId across the four levels the issue names.
8. src/api/routes.js is the composition point and the only place maturity is computed: one helper, extracted from GET /v1/metrics, now called by the metric route and by both issuance routes, and ONE providerForRequest helper is the single source of a request's failure injection for every write route.
9. src/web/pages.js stops being a shell, and src/web/client.js grows the decide fetch, the three-way response branch and the re-decide control.
10. scripts/seed.js writes four approval fixtures, five trust rows and a --reset-approvals affordance whose nonce list is built by CALLING decisionNonce over the same seeded id list, so no prefix literal is ever written twice.

THREE RULES CARRY THE WHOLE PLAN. A PREFIX LITERAL CANNOT DRIFT IF IT IS NEVER WRITTEN: decisionNonce is the single definition and both the decide route and the reset call it. A PREDICATE CANNOT BE DISAGREED WITH IF IT IS WRITTEN ONCE: isPendingApproval has four callers and one body, the roster is one exported array with two assertions over it (set equality with DECISION_CLASSES, and its pinned order), and killSwitches.activeFor answers for every scope the same way the write side writes them. And EVERY ASSERTION A QA READER COMPARES LITERALLY HAS A NAMED MECHANISM BEHIND IT: a method, a response field, a selector or a URL - which is the defect class the last four rounds each rejected, and the rule applied to every line of qa_script below.

Pure, no IO, no repository import. validateApproval(approval) rejects an action_class outside ACTION_CLASSES, a non-UTC or unparseable expires_at, a missing or blank impact or downside, and a constraints.delta_micros that is not a non-negative safe integer.

visibleReason(value) -> string|null. Trim, reject null, empty and whitespace, reject over 500 characters with REASON_TOO_LONG, and strip the invisible set [\\u200B-\\u200D\\u2060\\uFEFF] before the emptiness check so a zero-width-space-only reason is rejected the same way an empty one is. It then also requires at least one character that survives removing whitespace, the invisible set, and Unicode combining marks (\p{M}), because a reason made only of combining marks passes trim() and the client's identical check and then renders as an empty-looking input while the audit row records something. The stripped and trimmed text is what is stored, verbatim, and escapeHtml handles it on render.

isPendingApproval(row, {nowIso}) is THE predicate: status === 'pending' AND Date.parse(expires_at) > Date.parse(nowIso). An expires_at exactly equal to nowIso is NOT pending. Four consumers, one body: the decide route's rule (2), pages.js's partition, the seed reset's own reasoning, and the test counts.

partitionApprovals(rows, {nowIso}) -> {pending, executed, rejected, lapsed}, each bucket ordered (expires_at, approval_id) so the page is deterministic. 'lapsed' is a status of 'pending' whose expires_at is at or before nowIso - it is derived, never stored. NOTE WHAT THIS RETURNS AND DOES NOT: it buckets APPROVAL rows, so it cannot carry a receipt id, a reconciliation or a drift, because the approvals table has no such columns. The executed-receipts panel is therefore NOT driven by the executed bucket of this function; it is driven by repositories.actionRecords, and pages.js joins the two by approval_id. Stated here so the next reader does not try to render a receipt from a bucket that has none.

Pure domain module: no IO, no driver/provider/sqlite import, no process.env. Exports exactly these names and nothing else: DEFAULT_SIGNING_SECRET, ACTION_CLASSES, POLICY_ONLY_CLASSES, BAND_ORDER, POSTURE_LABELS, labelFor, decisionNonce, validateIntent, issueCapability, validateCapability, createKernel.

DEFAULT_SIGNING_SECRET is the dev-only literal 'dev-policy-signing-secret-not-a-production-secret'. It lives HERE and not in src/api/routes.js, so the route file holds no key material (an isolation test greps routes.js for it) while index.js stays the only reader of the POLICY_SIGNING_SECRET environment variable.

ACTION_CLASSES. The class SET is derived from a source of truth; the ORDER is a pin. Set = DECISION_CLASSES imported from src/domain/decisions.js:21-26 union exactly one explicit policy-only entry, 'new-geography'. The derivation is a MEMBERSHIP claim, not an order (DECISION_CLASSES is frozen with budget-change first while every rendered surface here pins campaign-status first), so the exported array is a pinned literal and test/policy/kernel.test.js asserts BOTH set equality with DECISION_CLASSES union {new-geography} AND that the array's order is exactly this literal. THE PINNED ORDER IS: campaign-status, budget-change, creative-refresh, new-geography, campaign-launch. pages.js renders in that order, AC-6 and qa_script compare positionally against it, and test/web/approvals.test.js asserts it cell by cell. Each entry carries {microLimitMicros, requiresMicrosConstraint, requiredMaturityBand, action}: campaign-status {50_000_000, constraint NOT permitted, 'emergency-only', set_campaign_status}; budget-change {50_000_000, micros REQUIRED, 'emergency-only', update_campaign_budget}; creative-refresh {10_000_000, not permitted, 'emergency-only', update_campaign_creative}; new-geography {0, not permitted, 'emergency-only', create_campaign, policy-only}; campaign-launch {0, not permitted, 'emergency-only', create_campaign}. POLICY_ONLY_CLASSES = ['new-geography'] so a caller can label a policy-only row.

decisionNonce(approvalId) -> 'apr_' + approvalId. THE SINGLE DEFINITION of the approval-decision nonce in the repository. The prefix literal appears inside this function and nowhere else. The decide route calls decisionNonce(approvalId); the seed reset builds its list by SEEDED_APPROVAL_IDS.map(decisionNonce); nothing writes 'apr_' or 'apr_seed_' by hand. test/policy/kernel.test.js pins the value with one assertion. Consequence to state plainly: the reset's deletion predicate is NOT a prefix match. It is a WHERE tenant_id = ? AND nonce IN (<that mapped list>), so it cannot disagree with the value the approve path stores whatever a later slice renames a fixture to.

validateIntent(intent, {nowIso, posture, approval, maturity}) -> {ok, intent} | {ok:false, error}. THE AUTONOMY GATE and the only place a write is admitted. Rules IN THIS ORDER, and the order is part of the contract - a class refused for want of an approval must never reach the band check.
  (a) intent.action_class must be in the roster, else AUTONOMY_NOT_EARNED with details.reason 'unknown-class'.
  (a2) intent.action must EQUAL the action the roster registers for that class, else AUTONOMY_NOT_EARNED with details.reason 'action-mismatch'. This sits BEFORE every approval rule. Without it the calibration story is unenforced at the only place it is enforced: the seed earns autonomy for campaign-status on a reversible action, and a caller posts {action_class:'campaign-status', action:'create_campaign'} and receives a signed envelope for a campaign creation under a posture the ledger never granted for anything irreversible. The two available enforcement points are refuse-the-mismatch and silently-overwrite-the-envelope-action. THIS PLAN PINS REFUSE, so a mis-paired intent is a visible 403 with a named reason. The test names campaign-status carrying create_campaign as the case that must fail.
  (b) A missing or unrecognised posture is a REFUSAL, never a default, and a malformed approval row is a refusal. Every ambiguous input fails closed (TR-24).
  (c) posture 'autonomous-under-micro-limits' with approval === null admits.
  (d) The SAME posture WITH an approval row present is ALSO ADMITTED, because an approval is additional authority and never a disqualifier, but the row is still validated when present, so one that does not cover this intent is refused with details.reason 'mismatch' (different action_class or resource), 'terminal' (status executed or rejected) or 'expired' (expires_at <= nowIso). Rule (d) exists because approving a class the seed calibrates autonomous is a real case, and leaving it undefined is how a wrong write happens in the highest-risk slice in the project.
  (e) ANY other posture ('approval-required', 'shadow', or the fail-closed no-row default) admits ONLY with an approval row present, unexpired at nowIso, non-terminal, and matching intent.action_class and intent.resource; otherwise the refusal names the failing condition 'no-approval', 'expired', 'terminal' or 'mismatch'. 'shadow' is IN this rule deliberately: shadow means NEVER AUTONOMOUS, not never possible. A human approval is the whole point of the approvals queue, and a reading in which a shadow-pinned class can never be approved makes the queue a dead end for the highest-risk class the product knows. IAC-4 asks that new-geography 'stays in shadow or approval', which is exactly this split.
  (f) THE MICRO-LIMIT, THEN THE BAND. MICRO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED when the intent's amount exceeds the class microLimitMicros, where the amount is constraints.delta_micros when it is a finite number and 0 otherwise. THE COMPARISON FOR A CLASS THAT DOES NOT REQUIRE A MICROS CONSTRAINT IS STATED BECAUSE A CRITERION RESTS ON IT: an absent constraints.delta_micros is 0 and the check is 0 <= microLimitMicros, so campaign-status with an empty constraints object is admitted, while a NEGATIVE delta_micros is MICRO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED on every class regardless of the flag. For budget-change, whose requiresMicrosConstraint is true, an absent, non-numeric, negative or non-integer delta_micros is ALSO MICRO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, because a missing number is not a small number and an absent constraint otherwise passes an upper-bound check by not existing.

RULE (f)'s BAND IS A FLOOR AND ITS DIRECTION IS NOT NEGOTIABLE. The intent's band is policyBand(maturity).label and the class's requiredMaturityBand is the LOWEST band permitted to act: admit iff BAND_ORDER.indexOf(actual) >= BAND_ORDER.indexOf(required), where BAND_ORDER = ['emergency-only','protective','moderate','strategic'] and labelFor(band) is exported alongside. policyBand is IMPORTED from src/domain/measurement.js rather than restated, and BAND_ORDER is the order its <0.35 / <0.70 / <0.90 edges already encode, so the gate and the metric surface cannot drift apart. A HIGHER band NEVER blocks: a class requiring 'protective' is ADMITTED at maturity 0.95, and a class requiring 'strategic' is refused for every maturity below 0.90, which coincides with policyBand's own gated flag. maturity 0.90 exactly is 'strategic' and is admitted, matching test/domain/measurement.test.js:106. A CEILING reading inverts the safety property: it would admit data at maturity 0 that the class declared too immature and refuse data at 0.95 that it declared ready. Note the doc drift, do not inherit it: docs/trd.md's TR-7 line writes '>0.90 strategic' where src/domain/measurement.js:244-259 and its pinned test say '>= 0.90'. The implementation wins, docs/ is out of bounds from a ticket branch, and the drift is filed in out_of_scope.

THE MATURITY ARGUMENT IS VALIDATED BEFORE IT IS USED, AND null IS ONE OF THE BAD VALUES. Anything that is not a finite number (undefined, null, NaN, a numeric string) is refused MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED with details {required, actual: null, maturity: null, reason: 'maturity-unknown'} BEFORE policyBand is called. null is explicitly in that set because the route's own computation substitutes 0 for a tenant with no events, and laundering 'no evidence' into a legitimate 0 is the same fail-open by a different door. maturity is a caller-supplied number and never an internal read: this module never touches a repository or a clock, so the ROUTE that supplies it owns the source and the doc comment says so.

issueCapability(intent, {secret, policyVersion, ttlMs, nowIso, expiresAtCap, nonce}) signs with node:crypto createHmac and returns {tenant, resource, action, constraints, maturity, band, expiry, nonce, policy_version} plus a capability_id, with expiry = min(now + ttlMs, expiresAtCap) and ttlMs 900_000. THE ENVELOPE CARRIES maturity AND band because they are properties of the gate decision and signing them is what makes the receipt's audit columns trustworthy: the executor copies them onto the action_records row, so the receipt records the band that was actually enforced on BOTH the autonomous and the approval path rather than null on the autonomous one. nonce is OPTIONAL and generated internally ('nce_' + 16 hex from randomUUID) only when omitted, which is what lets the decide route pass decisionNonce(approvalId) instead of a string it assembles itself.

validateCapability(capability, {secret, nowIso, killSwitches, nonces}) -> MALFORMED_CAPABILITY, BAD_SIGNATURE, EXPIRED_CAPABILITY, REPLAYED_NONCE, OVER_SCOPE (details name the violated constraint), KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE. Both injected ports are NON-MUTATING and read-only: killSwitches {isActive(tenantId, scope, scopeId)} and nonces {seen(tenantId, nonce)} where seen is never claim, because claiming a nonce is the executor's job and this module must never reserve one. createKernel({secret, policyVersion, ttlMs, killSwitches, nonces}) binds the ports and has the routes as their only callers. THE nonces PORT IS BOUND TO action_records, NOT TO capabilities: action_records carries UNIQUE (tenant_id, nonce) and holds a row only after a successful write, so seen is false for a freshly issued capability and true only for a nonce already spent. Binding it to capabilities would make seen true for every capability and validateCapability would answer REPLAYED_NONCE on every execution. REPLAYED_NONCE is therefore defence in depth that the executor's earlier dedupe shadows on the live path; the doc comment says so, and no one should 'fix' the duplicate answer into a 409 to make the branch reachable.

THE KILL-SWITCH CHECK, EXPLICITLY, because leaving it implicit is what made KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE and OVER_SCOPE unobservable: validateCapability evaluates FOUR scope keys, in this order, and refuses on the FIRST active one with details {scope, scope_id}. The keys are, and every one is derivable from the signed envelope with nothing added to it: ('global', envelope.tenant) - a global freeze is stored under the tenant that raised it, never under a '' sentinel - ('tenant', envelope.tenant), ('provider', 'meta_ads') - the sole provider this epic integrates, named as a constant here so the string is written once - and ('campaign', envelope.resource). A write is refused if any of the four is active, so a provider-wide freeze blocks a campaign write and a campaign-wide freeze blocks only that campaign. OVER_SCOPE is the sibling refusal and is what keeps a tenant's envelope from being executed against another tenant's resource: it is the combination of envelope.tenant not matching the caller's tenantId and a scope check that the envelope names. POSTURE_LABELS maps the three machine postures to the display strings the page renders and the criterion quotes: 'autonomous under micro-limits', 'approval required', 'shadow'.

Pure, no IO, no repository import. scoreFor(row) over a stored ledger row {evaluated, correct, needless, downside_penalties} and postureFor(actionClass, row, roster, pinned) -> 'autonomous-under-micro-limits' | 'approval-required' | 'shadow', with documented thresholds: autonomous requires evaluated >= 3 for that class AND precision (correct/evaluated) >= 0.90 AND false-intervention rate (needless/evaluated) <= 0.05 AND downside_penalties === 0. A pinned flag forces 'shadow' regardless of score, and a class with NO row is 'approval-required' (TR-24, fail closed), which is the only other path to that label and the reason the campaign-launch row of the table carries the 'no evidence' Why copy. recordOutcome(row, {outcome, needless, downside}) folds one evaluation into the next row. The two callers are the approvals page's posture table and kernel.validateIntent, both calling this one function, so the displayed posture and the enforced posture cannot disagree. The executor does NOT call it and must not: a signed capability is the attestation, and re-deriving posture at execute time would let a later trust-row edit retroactively invalidate a correctly issued capability.

createExecutor({repositories, provider, kernel, auditClock}). The ONLY module that calls a provider write method. execute(capability, {actor, tenantId}) runs its checks in THIS ORDER and the order is the contract.

(0) TENANT. The capability's own tenant field must equal the caller's tenantId, else {executed:false, error:{code:'TENANT_MISMATCH'}} with no write; the envelope is bearer material and the executor does not take the caller's word for it.

(1) DURABLE DEDUPE FIRST, in two sub-steps. (1a) If actionRecords.getByNonce(tenantId, nonce) already holds a row, return {executed:false, duplicate:true, receipt_id, reconciliation, drift} immediately, without validating through the kernel and without calling the provider; a duplicate mutates nothing, so it returns its receipt even while a kill switch is active. Stated in the doc comment so nobody 'fixes' it into a 409, because a second tab or a retried POST is exactly the case where a 409 tells the operator their action failed when it succeeded. (1b) ATOMIC CLAIM, repositories.idempotency.claim(tenantId, nonce, 'executor') before the provider call, using the primitive the repository already ships (:133-172, whose claim is INSERT OR IGNORE and so genuinely atomic, and the shape src/workflows/scheduler.js:71-79 already uses), so of two interleaved deliveries exactly one reaches the provider; a false return means another caller won, so return {executed:false, duplicate:false, error:{code:'EXECUTION_IN_PROGRESS', retryable:true}} with NO provider call and NO wait. Step 1a alone is check-then-act and does not close the two-tab race; 1b is what makes that claim true. The loser is told to retry rather than to wait on a receipt row, because a winner that then FAILS releases the claim (below) and no row is ever coming - a bounded wait on a row that may never appear is the trap this replaces.

(2) kernel.validateCapability, where the signature, expiry, scope, replay and kill-switch rejections happen, the last over the four scope keys named in the kernel entry. ANY REFUSAL HERE, AND ANY REFUSAL FROM (0), RELEASES the 1b CLAIM through repositories.idempotency.release(tenantId, nonce, 'executor') before returning. Nothing that did not reach the provider may leave a nonce burned.

(3) Resolve the write method from the capability's SIGNED action through the contract module's ACTION_WRITES map, never from anything the caller passes at execute time, and derive its arguments from the envelope through ONE named function, writeArgsFor(action, envelope). resource supplies the target id for update and status actions - the adset id for update_campaign_budget, the campaign id for set_campaign_status and update_campaign_creative. For create_campaign the resource is a PROPOSED id that does not exist yet and the name comes from envelope.constraints.name, NOT from resource: createCampaign takes {name} and mints its own id, so reading the name off resource would create a campaign literally called 'campaign_004'. constraints supply delta_micros for the budget action and the target status for the status action. This is stated because a previous revision left the mapping unsaid and an implementer then wrote a create against a resource the fake's fixtures do not contain. The SAME provider instance serves the write and the re-read in (4), so one request reconciles against the state it just wrote.

(4) Re-read provider state through the read interface. drift is classified: 'none' when the re-read agrees with the request and the provider reported no drift, otherwise the source the provider itself reports - 'manual', 'platform' or 'third-party'. reconciliation is a CLOSED VOCABULARY with the same treatment, because the receipt column, the toast and the failure panel all render it and only one of its values was ever named: 'agreed' when the post-write re-read reports exactly the requested state, 'diverged' when the re-read succeeded and reports something else, 'partial' when only some of a multi-field change landed, and 'unknown' when there is no re-read to compare against. The success path therefore yields 'agreed' on seeded data, which is the string qa_script step 3 and the successful-approve test case quote; 'unknown' is the provider-refusal value and the only one that reaches the failure panel. The fake reports drift only from a writeDrift option the tests inject, so 'none' is the only drift value reachable in a live QA run; that is filed in residual_risks rather than implied to be covered.

(5) Append the action_records receipt (repositories.actionRecords.append), record the idempotency effect, append an audit event carrying actor and capability id, and return {executed:true, receipt_id, requested, reported, reconciliation, drift}. THE RECEIPT COPIES maturity AND band FROM THE ENVELOPE onto maturity_at_decision and band_at_decision, which is why those columns are signed rather than recomputed: without this the two audit columns are null on every autonomous receipt and the receipt cannot answer which band was enforced.

A provider refusal (ok:false) RELEASES the claim through repositories.idempotency.release, returns {executed:false, duplicate:false, error, reconciliation:'unknown'}, writes NO action_records row and claims no nonce durably, so the caller's approval stays pending and a retry is a genuine retry rather than a swallowed claim. The provider is injected per request; the executor never constructs one. This module does not import trust.js and does not consult the ledger: a signed capability is the attestation and the gate has one owner.

An action absent from the map is a MALFORMED_CAPABILITY, not a fallthrough to a default. Every write returns the same {ok, ...} envelope the reads use, so the executor has one failure shape to handle: {ok:true, data} on success and {ok:false, error:{code, message, details}} on refusal, with the same codes the read path already returns (META_ERROR_PARAMS' FAILURE_MODES plus the provider's own).

The four WRITE_METHODS, against a per-instance deep copy of FIXTURES rather than the module constant, so a write in one request is not visible in the next - which is what makes AC-2's 'executes exactly once' observable only through the durable store and never through the provider, exactly as the routes.js:103 per-request construction implies. risks: This is a fourteen-file change that creates a write path, a trust ledger, a kill switch and a live approvals screen in one ticket, and the whole of it is new surface in the highest-risk part of the system. Nothing here is a refactor of something that already works; the only pre-existing behaviour at risk is the approvals screen and the dashboard's guardian panel, both of which are being replaced.

The three blocking defects this work order corrects were all the same shape as the ones the last four rounds were rejected for - an assertion with no mechanism behind it - and they were each found by re-reading the same files, not by new insight. A fourth round finding in the same family is therefore plausible, and the review stage on this route is where it should be caught.

POST /v1/actions/execute is a bearer-token surface whose only control is the signing secret, and that secret has a public dev default. A capability forged offline is accepted without the trust ledger ever being consulted, and the blast radius is bounded only by the fact that the only writable provider is an in-memory fake.

A ticket branch may not write .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md or environment.md, so those stay stale about the new data-testids, the new /v1 routes and the --reset-approvals re-run contract until the Librarian's branch is refreshed. qa_script is a substitute for them, not a replacement.

assumptions: The QA harness owns the server boot (.sdlc/config.yml:107 env.boot = npm run sdlc:serve) and can run `npm run sdlc:seed -- --reset-approvals` against the same ./data/app.db the running server has open, without unlinking the file and without restarting the server. What the code DOES settle: PRAGMA busy_timeout is per-connection, so placing it in openDatabase covers both the server and the seed process, and qa_script step 1 states the expected busy text so a lock is distinguishable from an empty queue.

Maturity for the gate is the tenant's data-through age computed over FUNNEL_TYPES-filtered raw events through the repo's own dataThrough/maturityFor/policyBand, in one helper extracted from GET /v1/metrics. On seed data the journey events are stamped by occurredAt() at scripts/seed.js:381, about six hours before the run, so maturity is about 0.0625 and reads 'emergency-only', which every seeded class requires and is therefore admitted. A tenant with NO events is not admitted at all: the helper returns null and the kernel refuses it as 'maturity-unknown'.

The approve path supplies the approval row it is executing to validateIntent, so a non-autonomous class is admitted by an explicit human approval and refused without one, and an autonomous class is admitted whether or not a row is supplied. This is also why the page renders no disabled approve button - a control that says 'you may not approve this' would contradict the rule the server enforces.

The seed's trust-ledger numbers (6/6/0/0 autonomous, 3/2/1/0 approval-required, two pinned shadow, one class with no row) are calibration fixtures chosen by this plan, and they are what make the enforced posture and the displayed posture agree. If a human wants different numbers the gate changes with them; what must not happen is the two surfaces being derived from different data, which is why both read trust.postureFor over the same rows and a test asserts the rendered table against the gate's own verdict.

An approval is created by strategy code in a later slice; this slice only decides, executes and records, so the seed and the tests are the only approval writers. This is also why nothing in this change can detect two pending approvals for the same resource - no component here proposes, so the duplicate case is deferred rather than solved.

A signed capability is valid on its own authority for its whole lifetime and is not re-checked against the trust ledger at execute time (see alternatives_considered for why a second owner is worse). One consequence is chosen rather than discovered: a capability issued before a freeze and executed after the re-enable is admitted, because validateCapability sees an inactive switch. That is recorded in residual_risks rather than left to be found.

The browser sends the tenant it rendered a card from, as data-tenant-id on the control and tenant_id in the decide body. resolveTenantId already accepts an explicit tenant and otherwise falls back to the sole tenant, or to 'tenant_demo' when two or more exist - so without this the moment a second tenant exists every browser decision 404s on a row that is genuinely pending, while the cross-tenant 404 test still passes and gives false confidence.

residual_risks: QA reads these first. (1) The provider-failure clause depends on both write routes calling one shared providerForRequest helper. That is now named in both, and a test asserts the approve route's ?meta_error=quota refusal over HTTP, so the two cannot drift - but the browser half of it still has no automated coverage and is qa_script step 5 only.

(2) The kill-switch clause depends on the write and read sides agreeing about scopes. activeFor now returns every scope for the tenant, freeze and reEnable share one pair of default literals, and a test asserts the agreement - but the four-scope enforcement is unit-tested through an injected port, and only the provider-scoped case is ever driven live.

(3) POST /v1/actions/execute is a bearer-token surface whose only control is the signing secret, and the secret has a public dev default, so a capability forged offline is accepted without the trust ledger ever being consulted; the blast radius is bounded only by the fact that the only writable provider is the in-memory fake.

(4) The executor's duplicate lookup runs BEFORE signature validation, deliberately, so that a redelivery under an active kill switch returns its receipt rather than a 409. The cost is that an unsigned POST naming a guessed nonce gets a receipt id back with no write performed.

(5) The two-step confirm, the retry safety, the meta_error forwarding and the three-way response branch are enforced SERVER-side because the repo has no DOM harness; the REST of client.js - the in-flight guard, the toast fill, the pending-count decrement, the reason input surviving a failure - has NO executable coverage and is verified by qa_script steps 3-7 only. Read those assertions as human observation, not as a regression net.
(6) The signing secret's dev default is live wherever POLICY_SIGNING_SECRET is unset, which today is everywhere.

(7) .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md and environment.md are NOT updated by this work order - a ticket branch may not touch them - and qa_script is a substitute, not a replacement. They stay stale about the new data-testids (guardian-banner, posture-table, posture-row-<action_class>, approval-card, approval-queue, approval-executed, executed-receipt, approval-lapsed, lapsed-row, approval-toast, approval-failed, approval-already-decided, approval-decision-result), the new /v1 routes and the --reset-approvals re-run contract until the Librarian's branch is refreshed.
(8) A capability issued before a freeze and executed after the re-enable is admitted, because validateCapability sees an inactive switch; nothing records that the capability predates the freeze.
(9) Two pending approvals for the same action_class and resource both execute - correct for this slice, since nothing here proposes, and asserted so a future dedupe is deliberate.

(10) No seeded class requires a band above 'emergency-only', so the live demo never exercises the maturity floor in its restrictive direction: it is covered by test/policy/kernel.test.js with explicit maturity fixtures, and a change to the band thresholds or to a class's requiredMaturityBand would NOT redden the live demo - only the kernel suite notices. The same is true of the micro-limits.

(11) The only drift value reachable in a live QA run is 'none', because the fake reports drift from an injected writeDrift option; manual, platform and third-party are unit-tested only. AC-2's 'the receipt carries the drift' is therefore half-live.

(12) The concurrent-decision loser is answered EXECUTION_IN_PROGRESS with retryable:true and lands in client.js's failure branch, so for the seconds while the winner is in flight that branch's 'nothing was executed' is literally true but reads like a failure. The server's own retryable message is shown beneath it, which is the mitigation; it is not a fourth panel.

(13) A kill switch raised between a page load and a click is enforced server-side but not reflected in the already-rendered page, so an operator can see a clean queue and be refused. The server is the authority and the banner is a convenience; a live indicator would need polling, which this slice does not add.

(14) A tenant with zero funnel events sees a 403 MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED on a card the page rendered as approvable, with no page-side signal that the account has no data yet. The posture table shows the classes but nothing ties the 403 to it.

The remedy is to delete ./data/app.db - and, now that WAL is on, its -wal and -shm sidecars - with the server stopped.

(16) A QA run that begins more than 24 hours after the last reset finds the three pending fixtures lapsed too, and every approval returns 409. The reset re-stamps them, which is why it is step 1; a run that skips it is not re-runnable for this reason alone.

(17) The action_records DELETE allowance is enforced by a test, not by a schema rule. A later slice that seeds a differently-named approval, or widens the deletion, reintroduces exactly the second-run failure the two-group reset stamp fixed, and nothing else in the suite would notice.

(18) The back-button case: client.js reloads the queue from the server after a success rather than removing the card optimistically, which is the right call, and the re-decide control is the truthful answer to a bfcache-rendered page landing with buttons still armed on a card that is already executed. What is not covered is back after a FAILURE panel: the typed reason lives only in the input, so a back/forward pair re-renders the queue from the server and the unsaved reason is gone. That is ordinary browser behaviour for unsaved form state, not a defect, and no test asserts either way.

(19) The dashboard's guardian panel now lists incidents, so the sentence 'No guardian incidents in the last 24 hours.' survives only in the no-incidents branch - which is the branch a seeded-but-unfrozen database takes. A test or QA note that matched that sentence as a literal will still match, and should not be read as the panel being unchanged.

(20) The posture table's first column now reads roster slugs ('campaign-status') where it read prose ('Campaign status change'), and the new-geography and campaign-launch rows both read approval-required with different Why copy. Nothing asserts the prose, so no test catches a future copy regression; the change is recorded here for the Librarian to reconcile against docs/ui.md.

(21) The five-state shells, the 404 envelope for unknown /v1 paths and the fake provider's cross-request statelessness are contracts this change edits or extends; test/web/approvals.test.js, test/api/*.test.js and test/integrations/meta_ads.test.js cover them explicitly, so read those assertions as the regression net rather than trusting this description.

(22) The null-scope posture table - five rows, all approval required, no evidence - is what a tenantless database renders, and the null-tenant guardian banner returns an empty string. work_order.confidence_rationale: The root cause is verified against the repository and not in doubt: there is no src/policy/, no src/executor/, no guardian, MIGRATIONS closes at 005, openDatabase sets no PRAGMA, createRepositories builds exactly thirteen repositories, and the approvals page is the static shell both prior documents describe. The three blocking defects this work order corrects I re-checked myself, at the lines the critique cited, and all three hold: routes.js:37 and :100-102 confirm the failure-injection convention has exactly one consumer today and the approve route named none; the write side defaults freeze to ('provider','meta_ads') while activeFor was specified over only the global and tenant disjuncts, so the row the demo writes was invisible to the banner, to GET /v1/guardian and to every other reader, and the envelope carries no scope for the four-key kill-switch check to read; and the reset re-stamped all four fixtures to now+24h while resetToSeed returns every one of them to status 'pending', so the lapsed fixture came back pending and step 2 of the QA script contradicted step 1 of the same script. Each is a naming defect rather than a design error, and each is now closed with a mechanism and a test case behind it. What holds the number at 71 rather than in the eighties is two things, neither of them a guess about the design. First, the base rate: this is the fifth round, the last four were each rejected for the same family - an assertion with no mechanism behind it - and the critique found three more instances of it in v13 plus five majors, all of them found by re-reading the same files rather than by any new insight about the problem. A fourth round finding in that family is plausible and should be priced in rather than argued away, and it is why I did not simply carry the proposal's own 74 forward. Second, the one thing that gates every browser criterion - whether the QA harness can pass --reset-approvals to a seed process writing to a database the running server holds open - cannot be verified from the code at all, and a fail there makes the whole browser half observable once per database. The diff is also fourteen files and four new modules, large relative to how much of it any single test touches. What would move it up: an implementer writing test/policy/kernel.test.js and test/api/approvals.test.js first and finding that the band floor, the finite-and-null maturity refusals, the four-scope kill-switch check, the autonomous-plus-approval case, the action binding, the atomic claim, the receipt-before-status ordering, the three-way response branch and the two-group reset stamp all hold together. What would move it down: QA discovering it cannot reset against the live server's open handle, or a second tenant appearing in a demo database and 404ing every browser decision.
work_order.debate_summary:
The critique was right more often than not, and I am not going to dress that up. I re-checked every finding against the file and line it cited, and I confirmed all nine against the code rather than accepting the citations. Three blocking findings hold and all three are folded in with the mechanism named, plus five majors. The first blocker is the same defect the previous round was corrected for, recurring one route over: the proposal named the failureMode source for POST /v1/actions/execute and left the approve route saying only 'a provider built for this request', so an implementer following it literally builds that provider with the default 'ok', the write succeeds, and the failure half of AC-5 - the clause the recorded rejection was about - can never be observed. I went past the critique's suggestion and made it one providerForRequest(request) helper that the page loop and both write routes call, so the convention has a single home and a third route cannot forget it. The second blocker is new to this round and is a regression the proposal introduced: v12 defaulted freeze to scope 'global', which the two-disjunct activeFor read actually matched; v13 changed the default to ('provider','meta_ads') to exercise a real level of the four the issue names, and left activeFor over only global and tenant rows. The row the demo writes is therefore invisible to the banner, to GET /v1/guardian and to the test that asserts the freeze is readable - AC-3 unobservable end to end - and the same gap leaves the kernel's isActive port with no caller, since the envelope carries no scope. I widened the read to every scope bound to the tenant rather than narrowing the write back to global, because defaulting to 'global' would make the demo exercise the one scope whose semantics need no testing, and I named the four scope keys the check evaluates so OVER_SCOPE and KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE have a defined path. The third blocker is a self-inflicted one: the reset re-stamped all four fixtures to now+24h while resetToSeed returns every one of them to status 'pending', so the lapsed fixture came back pending. Since step 1 IS the reset, every run failed at step 2. The fix restores the two groups differently - three pending at now+24h, the lapsed one at its original past stamp - and makes the summary print the two counts separately so '4 rows restored' is never read as '4 pending'. The four majors all hold: the executed-receipts panel rendered a receipt id, reconciliation and drift out of partitionApprovals, which buckets approval rows and neither the page entry nor the schema holds a single one of those three values; reconciliation had exactly one defined value ('unknown', on the refusal path) while drift had a closed vocabulary, an asymmetry that is omission rather than scoping; AC-1's how_to_verify told QA to run a pure module and count writes on a provider that module does not have, and said 'seven refusal cases' against a six-item check; and the pages.js entry never said the pending card's buttons were RENAMED from data-action approve/reject, never assigned the approval-card testid its own test and count depend on, and left client.js reading data-approval-id 'on the control or its row' - an ambiguity that ships a button bound to nothing. All four are fixed with the contract stated once on the page side and quoted by the client. The minor on the geography fixture's resource is real and I took the critique's second option rather than its first: the name comes from constraints.name, because resource is a proposed id for a create and reading the name off it would have created a campaign literally called 'campaign_004'. The minor on the inconsistent `verify` fields is cosmetic and I simply filled them all in rather than arguing about the field's meaning.

WHAT I DISMISSED, EXPLICITLY. Four things. The critique's proposal to re-gate the execute path against the trust ledger is the same suggestion the previous round declined, and I decline it again for the reason the plan already gave: a trust row edited between issuance and execution must not retroactively invalidate a correctly signed capability, so a legitimate write would fail for a reason the signer cannot see. Its regression note that the dashboard's guardian panel string now survives only in the no-incidents branch is correct but is not a defect - the plan already keeps that sentence in exactly that branch, and I have said so in residual_risks so nobody reads a passing test as the panel being unchanged. Its note that the /v1/metrics route now holds two maturity values is a real shape but the plan already pins both halves in a single test case, so the surfaces cannot quietly converge. And its back-after-a-failure-panel edge case is not a defect at all: the typed reason was never saved, so losing it on a back/forward pair is ordinary browser behaviour for unsaved form state, and inventing a test for it would assert nothing. I also did not adopt its suggestion to enforce the deterministic recovery predicate, which both prior rounds declined and which would make AC-3 permanently unreachable on seed data.

WHAT I ADDED THAT NEITHER DOCUMENT NAMED. Four things, and the first two are the ones I would most want a human to check. The executed panel's data source has a consequence neither document reached: once the panel is correctly driven by action_records rather than by approval rows, the autonomous receipt minted at qa_script step 9 - null approval_id, not in the reset's purge list - would appear in a panel that otherwise counts decisions taken on the queue, and would make step 12's 'ZERO executed receipts' false on the second run of the script. Filtering the panel to approval-backed receipts is what makes the criterion and the reset agree, and that is now in the page entry, the test case and step 12. Second, the renderPage-level guardian banner is a live crash on the existing suite: renderPage resolves tenant through firstTenant, which returns null on an empty store, and test/web/pages.test.js sweeps all five routes in all five states against a null-tenant repository. A `tenant.id` dereference in a banner composed above the page body throws outside the page function, where the page loop cannot catch it, and reddens every existing page test rather than just /approvals. The guard is now specified and a case asserts the whole sweep. Third, the re-enable route's scope had no default while the trigger route's did, and qa_script steps 9 and 11 disagreed with each other about the body - the same defaults now live in guardian.js where a test can compare them. And fourth, the reason validator's invisible-character set is extended to combining marks, because a reason made only of them passes trim() and the client's identical check and then renders as an empty-looking input while the audit row records something.

WHERE I DIFFER FROM THE PROPOSER. I kept the proposal's architecture, its pinned values and its rule ordering, and I rewrote nothing for style. What I changed is every place a criterion named an outcome the plan did not make reachable, and I changed them by naming the mechanism, not by weakening the criterion - including the two places where the honest answer was to widen a read rather than narrow a claim, and one place (the executed panel) where the only consistent answer required a new repository method, listByApproval, that the proposal had not thought to need. I also declined to carry its confidence of 74 upward. The number describes this work order, and the critique's three blockers were live in the document I was handed, which is direct evidence that 74 was optimistic about the class of defect this plan keeps producing.

THE HONEST SUMMARY OF THIS ROUND. Six rounds in, the pattern has not changed: this artifact keeps producing assertions with no mechanism behind them, and every round's corrections have come from re-reading the same files rather than from any new insight about the problem. Three of this round's findings are that class again, and two of them are the previous round's own correction failing to travel one route or one repository method over - which is the most useful thing to know about it, because it means the failure mode is omission at the edges, not misjudgement at the centre. I would not read a 71 as the plan being nearly wrong. I would read it as a large change in the highest-risk part of this system, correctly diagnosed, with every defect I know how to find closed and named, and with a real chance of a class I do not still open. The route carries a review stage; the argument for taking it seriously is stronger after this round, not weaker.

review.title: The rewritten approvals() dropped the `state === 'empty'` guard, so /approvals?state=empty renders the live queue instead of the empty shell. All four sibling page bodies still carry that guard (pages.js:344, :582, :767, :856) and main's approvals() had it too, so this is a regression against both the siblings and the previous revision, and it breaks the five-states contract every screen in this repo is held to.

All four sibling page bodies still carry that guard (pages.js:344, :582, :767, :856) and main's approvals() had it too, so this is a regression against both the siblings and the previous revision, and it breaks the five-states contract every screen in this repo is held to.

`src/web/pages.js:998`

Evidence: Rendered every route with override 'empty' against a SEEDED repository (one tenant, 3 pending approvals, 1 lapsed, 1 executed receipt):

  /               state=empty tenant=none empty-shell=true  cards=0
  /journal        state=empty tenant=none empty-shell=true  cards=0
  /opportunities  state=empty tenant=none empty-shell=true  cards=0
  /experiments    state=empty tenant=none empty-shell=true  cards=0
  /approvals      state=empty tenant=none empty-shell=FALSE cards=2

Live over HTTP, `GET /approvals?state=empty` emits `body[data-state="empty"]`, a header reading 'No connected account', and then two real [data-testid=approval-card] rows, a real lapsed-row and a real executed-receipt panel naming a live receipt id. /approvals is the only route whose empty state does not appear.

No test catches it, and the reason is instructive: test/web/pages.test.js:51-56 and test/web/approvals.test.js:269 sweep the five states against a NULL-tenant repository, where `rows = []` makes `pending.length === 0` and the empty state renders anyway. The only test that asserts approvals-empty (test/web/approvals.test.js:219) does so via a drained queue, not via override 'empty'. The fixture masks the missing guard.

This breaks .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md:7 ('No connected account' when empty) and :12 (approvals-empty is the per-page empty state), and docs/ui.md's per-screen five states.

Fix: Restore the guard in approvals() alongside the loading and error branches, before line 998:

  if (state === 'empty') {
    return emptyState({ title: 'No pending approvals', message: '...', testid: 'approvals-empty' });
  }

...and add a test that renders /approvals with override 'empty' against a repository that HAS a tenant with pending rows, asserting approvals-empty is present and approval-card is absent. The existing null-tenant sweep cannot catch this class of regression on its own.
